GPs and Psychiatrists read the same case history, but interpret the information differently and arrive at different diagnostic and management plans.
GPs and psychiatry trainees use similar diagnostic processes but with some differences.
GPs recognize the need to consider psychiatric disorders early in their clinical reasoning process but are cautious about making a definitive diagnosis.

the clinical decision-making of GPs in the management of mental health problems.
the processes of diagnosis and decision making in the treatment of patients presenting with psychological symptoms to general practitioners in the UK.
how GPs and psychiatry residents make clinical decisions and reach diagnoses in patients presenting with psychological symptoms and distress.

GPs and psychiatry are both reading from the same diagnostic book, but on different pages.

the diagnostic processes of general practitioners and psychiatrists are not identical, and that this may have significant implications for the management of patients presenting with psychological symptoms in general practice.

GPs do not make psychiatric diagnoses, but they do diagnose psychiatric disorders, and do so in the context of a broader understanding of their patient's presenting problem and the context in which it is presented.
